Most of the fix is fine (Rule 1 mixed-case preservation, Rule 2's first/last-word capitalization, and switching from `.capitalize()` to explicit first-char uppercasing are all correctly derived from the docstring). The problem is the new `is_after_colon` branch:

```python
is_after_colon = index > 0 and ":" in words[index - 1]
if is_first or is_last or is_after_colon:
    ...
```

Nothing in the docstring mentions colons or "words following a word ending in `:`" as a trigger for capitalizing an otherwise-lowercase small word. The docstring's rule 2 is explicit: a small word is lowercased "unless it is the first or the last word of `text`" — full stop, referring to the whole input, not to segments after punctuation. This branch was added purely to make `test_subtitle_after_colon` ("notes from the field: a year of remote work" → "...Field: A Year...") pass, and it directly contradicts the documented behavior rather than following from it.

The teammate was explicit: "the docstrings are the source of truth" and "don't change the tests." If the docstring and a test genuinely disagree (which appears to be the case here), the right move is to flag that conflict rather than silently bolt on undocumented behavior to force the test green. As written, the code now does something its own docstring doesn't describe, which will confuse future maintainers and makes the "docstring as spec" contract meaningless.

Please either:
1. Update the docstring to explicitly document the colon-boundary rule (so code and docs agree), and confirm with the team that this is actually the intended behavior for subtitles, or
2. Raise the discrepancy with the teammate instead of quietly special-casing it.

Requesting changes until the docstring/behavior mismatch is resolved.
